restatement: The card adds nine list-shaping filters (join, length, first, last, sort, unique, slice, lines, json) as rows of the collection group in the single filter registry. They must stay deterministic and free of eval. List filters coerce their input exactly as FOR does, and missing input counts as an empty list. sort must be stable, ordering numbers, then strings by code unit, then everything else, and sort=key must order objects by that key. unique keeps first occurrences. json prints compact JSON with sorted keys and rejects cycles. Every bad or undeclared parameter, and every object given to a list filter, must be a located type-error in both modes. The card must not change existing test expectations, add a runtime dependency or compile template-supplied regular expressions.
brief_mismatch: The reviewer-brief rubric limits scope to filters-collection.ts and its test file, but files_scope also grants docs/ephemeral/cycles/language/deltas. The manifest lists tests/language/filters-collection.test.ts as 'add', yet the diff shows it as an existing file being modified (index 2e536da..d6b8e32), so the file was not new to this card. The card's must-not reads 'change any existing test expectation other than the one named amendment (if any)', but criterion m1 drops that exception and no amendment is named anywhere.
verification_plan: c1: for each of join, length, first, last, slice, lines and unique, confirm tests cover an array, a comma string, a JSON-array string, a number or boolean, an object, an empty list, null and undefined, and that the code coerces through the same function FOR uses (tryCoerceToArray).

c1: confirm length counts list items, text characters (no coercion) and object keys; that join needs a separator and allows join=""; that slice follows Array.prototype.slice and accepts only integer-text bounds; and that lines splits on CRLF, CR and LF and drops one trailing empty item.
c1/m4: confirm an object given to join/first/last/sort/unique/slice is a type-error located at the variable in both lenient and strict mode, never a silent empty result.

c2: confirm sort is stable (a test with equal keys), numbers compare numerically, strings by code unit with no localeCompare, mixed lists put numbers before strings, other values keep their original order, and sort=key puts items without the key last; confirm the comparator is consistent for every input it can receive.
c2: confirm unique keeps first occurrences, tells 1 from '1' and 0 from false, and compares objects by stable JSON text that ignores key order.

c3: confirm json is compact with keys sorted by code unit at every depth, prints null for null or missing, raises a located type-error for a cyclic value without stack overflow, and accepts a shared non-cyclic reference.
c3/m4: confirm every collection filter rejects an undeclared parameter as a located type-error in render, validate and analyze, in both modes.
m1: confirm no existing test file is edited, the frozen test file included.
m2: confirm no new import from a third-party package.
m3: confirm every regex is a code literal and no template text reaches eval, Function or RegExp.
Rubric: confirm no filter name is listed outside the registry rows, nothing is changed outside files_scope, and no comparison or stable-JSON logic is duplicated.
Mutation: confirm no filter mutates its input array or objects.

findings.title: The builder edited the frozen test file without a logged scope exception or a named amendment

The edit makes the test match its name, but the builder changed a plan-owned test unilaterally, no scope exception is logged, and the card's 'named amendment' clause names none. If the original strict-default call was intended, the test now asserts different behavior from what was frozen.

findings.title: An object passed as JSON text (the n8n mapping form) silently becomes an empty list in every mode, unlike FOR

serves.scenario: n8n mapping values reach the core as strings, so an object mapped into a variable arrives as text such as '{"a":1}'. tryCoerceToArray returns null for a string starting with '{'. toList throws only when typeof input === 'object', so for this string it returns []. join prints '', first and last print nothing, and sort, unique and slice give [], with ok true even in strict mode. FOR raises TypeError in strict mode for the same non-coercible value, so this is not 'coerced exactly as FOR coerces', and the author's mistake passes silently.

findings.rubric: goal-critical: does ... an object given to a list filter fail with a located type-error in every mode, never silently? / do string inputs coerce exactly as FOR coerces them?
findings.reproduction: render('${{ v | join="," }}', { v: '{"a":1}' }, { standaloneLines: false, strictMode: true }) returns ok true and output ''. Reading: toList calls tryCoerceToArray, which returns null for a '{'-prefixed string (module page, Coercion), and the object check fails because typeof is 'string', so it falls through to return []. Compare FOR over the same value in strict mode, which throws TypeError (module page, Interpreting/FOR). Smallest fix: in toList, treat any non-null, non-undefined input that tryCoerceToArray rejects as the 'needs a list' error, and add a test row for a JSON-object string.
evidence: test:fc-collection: %s rejects an object input as a type-error saying a list is needed

findings.title: sort's numeric comparator is inconsistent for NaN and for equal infinities, so the order becomes engine-defined

serves.scenario: compare returns (a - b) for every number. NaN - x is NaN, which Array.prototype.sort treats as 0, so NaN counts as equal to every number while those numbers still order among themselves. That breaks transitivity, and the resulting order is implementation-defined, so a headless-core caller passing [3, NaN, 1] can get different output on different engines or versions. Infinity - Infinity also yields NaN. The project requires sort to be deterministic.

findings.rubric: goal-critical: does any collection filter give a different result for the same input on two runs, or depend on ... platform (sort, unique, json)?
findings.reproduction: COLLECTION_FILTERS.find(f => f.name === 'sort').apply([3, NaN, 1, 2], {}): the comparator calls compare(3, NaN) = NaN (treated as 0) and compare(3, 1) = 2, which is inconsistent, so ECMAScript leaves the result order implementation-defined. Smallest fix: give NaN a fixed place (for example, rank it with the 'other' values or after all numbers) and compare with < and > instead of subtraction, plus a test row containing NaN.

findings.title: textOf copies the output step's text rule instead of reusing it

serves.scenario: join must print each item 'as the output step prints it'. textOf re-implements that rule, and its own comment says it is 'the same rule as valueToText in filters.ts'. If the output step's text form changes, join silently diverges from it.

findings.rubric: polish: is the new code small, free of a second filter list, and free of duplicated comparison or stable-JSON logic?
findings.reproduction: Read core/src/filters-collection.ts:6-10. The comment points to valueToText in filters.ts, and the body is a separate copy. Smallest change: import and reuse the output step's function, exporting it if needed.

findings.title: length counts UTF-16 code units, which the contract calls 'characters', and no test uses non-BMP text

serves.scenario: c1 and the spec say length counts the 'characters of a text', while the same contract says 'code unit' wherever it means code units (sort, json). input.length returns 2 for a single emoji, so an author counting characters in a prompt gets a different number from what the contract wording promises. The lead should settle the wording or the behavior.

findings.reproduction: COLLECTION_FILTERS.find(f => f.name === 'length').apply('\uD83D\uDE00', {}) returns 2, while the input is one character. No row in the frozen test covers a non-BMP character.
